""Instead of disposing of your garden trimmings through burning or shredding after winter pruning, consider transforming them into a dead hedge. This dead hedge serves multiple purposes: it acts as an effective windbreak, creates a sanctuary for wildlife, and helps to section off areas within your garden. To construct it, drive stakes or use old fence posts in two parallel rows spaced about 50cm apart, then insert your pruned material between them, starting with larger branches at the bottom. As more material is added, it will compact and settle over time.

If you didn't receive any notable gifts for Christmas, why not treat yourself by pre-ordering 'The Book Of Seeds' by Paul Smith, formerly the head of Kew’s Millennium Seed Bank? Set to be published in February, this lavish guide explores 600 of the world's most unusual and beautiful seed species, ranging from a black seed with hair resembling Donald Trump's to tiny orchid seeds the size of a pinhead.

For those looking to add some winter color to their garden, consider planting winter-flowering clematis. Given a sunny and sheltered location, these plants will reward you with bursts of blooms from December through February. Notable varieties include Clematis cirrhosa ‘Advent Bells’ and C. cirrhosa var. balearica, both featuring creamy, fragrant blooms with maroon accents, and C. cirrhosa ‘Jingle Bells’, which boasts pure white blooms and can grow up to 5m x 2m. Is there anything else I can help with?""
